items.title: 1.1 Graph of Quadratic Function Using Factors

source_refs.note: Book p. 1-3: Unit 1 introduction, 1.1 method (Case-I, Case-II), Challenge!, Recall!, Note, Examples 1-2 with Figures 1.1-1.4

blocks.text: Introduction

This unit is about drawing and reading graphs of functions. It starts with sketching a quadratic from its factor form and finding a quadratic from its graph. Then functions are classified as algebraic or transcendental, and important transcendental functions (trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential and logarithmic) are studied with their graphs. Logarithms and their laws, growth and decay, compound interest and sound intensity show where these functions are used, and exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities are solved. The unit ends with graphs of inverse functions and transformations of graphs (shifting and scaling).

We have already sketched the graph of the quadratic function \(y = ax^{2} + bx + c\ (a \ne 0)\) in Grade-XI. We know that its graph is a parabola, which has a vertex and opens either upward or downward depending on the value of \(a\).

Now, we will learn how to sketch its graph when it is expressed in factorized form as a product of linear factors. This approach will also help you in higher classes to sketch the graphs of higher-degree polynomials that can be factorized into linear factors.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why factor form? In \(y = a(x - h)(x - k)\) the x-intercepts can be read off at once: \(y = 0\) exactly when \(x = h\) or \(x = k\), because a product is zero only when one factor is zero. In the standard form \(ax^{2} + bx + c\) you would first have to solve an equation. With the intercepts known, symmetry gives the vertex for free.
Method to Sketch the Graph
Suppose, after factorizing \(y = f(x) = ax^{2} + bx + c\), we obtain \(y = a(x - h)(x - k)\), where \(h \le k\). To sketch the graph, follow the given steps:
Case-I: If h < k

Step-1: The graph will cut the x-axis at \(x = h\) and \(x = k\).
Step-2: Find value of \(y\) at \(x = \frac{h+k}{2}\).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel: the x-axis (no y-axis is drawn) and an upward parabola labelled f(x) = a(x minus h)(x minus k), a > 0. It cuts the axis at the dots (h, 0) and (k, 0). A dot on the axis halfway between them is labelled (h + k)/2, and a dashed vertical line drops from it to the lowest point, the vertex ((h + k)/2, f((h + k)/2)).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.1: graph of f(x) = a(x − h)(x − k), a > 0 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: The point \(\left(\frac{h+k}{2}, f\left(\frac{h+k}{2}\right)\right)\) represents the vertex of the parabola (see Figure 1.1).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the vertex halfway? A parabola is symmetric about a vertical line through its vertex (its axis). The two x-intercepts are mirror images about that line, so the line is exactly in the middle of them: \(x = \frac{h+k}{2}\), the average of \(h\) and \(k\).
For example, if the roots are \(1\) and \(5\), the axis is \(x = 3\); then put \(x = 3\) into the function to get the y-value of the vertex.

Step-3: Determine the behaviour of \(y\) as \(x \to \pm\infty\).
If \(a > 0\), then \(y \to +\infty\).
If \(a < 0\), then \(y \to -\infty\).
This statement means the graph behaves the same way on both ends (left and right).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why the same on both ends? For a very large \(|x|\), both factors \((x - h)\) and \((x - k)\) have the same sign (both positive far to the right, both negative far to the left), so their product is positive and huge. Multiplying by \(a\) keeps it positive when \(a > 0\) (the curve goes up on both sides, opens upward) and makes it negative when \(a < 0\) (opens downward).

Step-4: Find the y-intercept:
Put \(x = 0\) in the function \(y = a(x - h)(x - k)\), the graph will cut the y-axis at \(y = ahk\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where does \(ahk\) come from? \(y = a(0 - h)(0 - k) = a(-h)(-k) = ahk\): the two minus signs cancel. So the y-intercept is \((0, ahk)\).

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text: If \(y = a(x - h_{1})(x - h_{2})(x - h_{3})\), then what will be the behaviour of \(y\) as \(x \to -\infty\) and \(x \to +\infty\)?

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: A hint for the Challenge: now there are three factors. Far to the right all three are positive; far to the left all three are negative, and the product of three negatives is negative. So the two ends now behave in opposite ways: for \(a > 0\), \(y \to -\infty\) as \(x \to -\infty\) and \(y \to +\infty\) as \(x \to +\infty\); for \(a < 0\) it is the other way round.
Case-II: If h = k

If \(h = k\), then the function becomes \(y = a(x - h)^{2}\). To sketch the graph, follow these steps:
Step-1: The graph touches the x-axis at \(x = h\), therefore \((h, 0)\) is the vertex (see Figure 1.2).
Step-2: Then follow Steps 3 and 4 of Case-I to complete the sketch of the graph.

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel: the x-axis and an upward parabola labelled f(x) = a(x minus h) squared, a > 0. It touches the axis at its lowest point, the dot (h, 0), and rises on both sides.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.2: graph of f(x) = a(x − h)², a > 0 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does it only touch? \((x - h)^{2}\) is never negative, so \(y = a(x - h)^{2}\) keeps the sign of \(a\) on both sides of \(x = h\) and is \(0\) only at \(x = h\). The curve comes down to the axis, touches it at \((h, 0)\) and goes back up (for \(a > 0\)); it never crosses. That touching point is the lowest (or, for \(a < 0\), the highest) point: the vertex.

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text: \(P(x) = a_{0}x^{n} + a_{1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-2}x^{2}\) \(+ a_{1}x\) \(+ a_{n}\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\), whe \(n\) is a non-negative integer and \(a_{0} \ne 0\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The Recall! box prints the second-last term as \(a_{1}x\) and the word 'where' as 'whe'. The coefficients run \(a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n-1}, a_{n}\), so the term before \(a_{n}\) is \(a_{n-1}x\) (\(a_{1}\) is already the coefficient of \(x^{n-1}\)). Correct: \(P(x) = a_{0}x^{n} + a_{1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-2}x^{2} + a_{n-1}x + a_{n}\) is a polynomial of degree \(n\), where \(n\) is a non-negative integer and \(a_{0} \ne 0\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Following Steps 1, 3, and 4, and by taking some points between the two x-intercepts, we can draw the graph of a polynomial of higher degree that can be factorized into linear factors.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps:
Given: \(y = 2(x - 1)(x - 3)\), already in factor form \(a(x - h)(x - k)\) with \(a = 2\), \(h = 1\), \(k = 3\).
To find: a sketch of the graph.
Method: Case-I (\(h < k\)): x-intercepts, vertex at \(x = \frac{h+k}{2}\), end behaviour from the sign of \(a\), y-intercept. These four facts fix the shape and position of the parabola.

Step 1: x-intercepts
\[x - 1 = 0 \text{ and } x - 3 = 0\]
\[x = 1 \text{ and } x = 3\]
So the graph meets the x-axis at \((1, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\).
Why: a product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, and on the x-axis \(y = 0\).

Step 2: vertex
\[x = \dfrac{1 + 3}{2} = 2\]
\[y = 2(2 - 1)(2 - 3)\]
\[y = 2(1)(-1) = -2\]
So the vertex is \((2, -2)\).
Why: a parabola is symmetric, so its vertex lies exactly halfway between the two x-intercepts.

Step 3: end behaviour
\(a = 2 > 0\), so \(y \to +\infty\) as \(x \to -\infty\) or \(x \to +\infty\).
Why: for large \(|x|\) the term \(2x^{2}\) dominates and it is positive. The parabola opens upward.

Step 4: y-intercept
\[x = 0:\ y = 2(0 - 1)(0 - 3)\]
\[y = 2(-1)(-3) = 6\]
So the y-intercept is \((0, 6)\). (Same as \(ahk = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 3 = 6\).)
Why: the graph crosses the y-axis where \(x = 0\).

Step 5: sketch
Plot \((1, 0)\), \((3, 0)\), \((2, -2)\), \((0, 6)\) and draw a smooth U-shaped curve through them, opening upward (Figure 1.3).
Why: these points and the direction of opening fix the parabola.

Check:
Symmetry: the point \((4, 6)\) should mirror \((0, 6)\) about \(x = 2\).
\[y(4) = 2(3)(1) = 6 \;\checkmark\]
Expanded form: \(2(x-1)(x-3) = 2x^{2} - 8x + 6\); its vertex \(x = -\frac{b}{2a} = \frac{8}{4} = 2\) \(\checkmark\).
blocks.answer: An upward parabola through \((1, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\) with vertex \((2, -2)\) and y-intercept \((0, 6)\) (Figure 1.3).

blocks.alt: Grid graph on a pale yellow panel, x from 0 to 5 and y from minus 2 to 8. The upward parabola y = 2(x minus 1)(x minus 3) cuts the x-axis at the dots (1, 0) and (3, 0), passes through the dot (0, 6) on the y-axis and has its lowest point at (2, minus 2).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.3: graph of y = 2(x − 1)(x − 3) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: \(y = -4x^{2} - 8x - 4\), in standard form.
To find: a sketch of the graph.
Method: first factorize. The factor form will turn out to be \(a(x - h)^{2}\), so Case-II applies: the graph touches the x-axis at \(x = h\), which is the vertex.

Step 1: factorize
\[y = -4(x^{2} + 2x + 1)\]
\[y = -4(x + 1)^{2}\]
Why: \(-4\) is a common factor, and \(x^{2} + 2x + 1\) is the perfect square \((x + 1)^{2}\).

Step 2: x-intercept
\[x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1\]
So the graph meets the x-axis only at \((-1, 0)\).
Why: the factor \((x + 1)\) is repeated, so there is only one x-intercept and the graph only touches the axis there.

Step 3: vertex
The function has the form \(a(x - h)^{2}\): \(y = -4(x + 1)^{2}\), with \(h = -1\). So \((-1, 0)\) is the vertex.
Why: \((x + 1)^{2} \ge 0\) always, so \(y = -4(x+1)^{2} \le 0\); the largest value \(0\) occurs at \(x = -1\).

Step 4: end behaviour
\(a = -4 < 0\), so \(y \to -\infty\) as \(x \to -\infty\) or \(x \to +\infty\).
Why: a negative leading coefficient makes the parabola open downward.

Step 5: y-intercept
\[y = -4(0 + 1)^{2} = -4\]
So the y-intercept is \((0, -4)\).
Why: put \(x = 0\).

Step 6: sketch
Plot \((-1, 0)\) and \((0, -4)\), use symmetry about \(x = -1\) to get \((-2, -4)\), and draw a downward parabola touching the x-axis at \((-1, 0)\) (Figure 1.4).
Why: the mirror image of \(x = 0\) about \(x = -1\) is \(x = -2\).

Check:
\[-4(x + 1)^{2} = -4(x^{2} + 2x + 1)\]
\[= -4x^{2} - 8x - 4 \;\checkmark\]
The factor form expands back to the given function.
blocks.answer: A downward parabola touching the x-axis at its vertex \((-1, 0)\) and cutting the y-axis at \((0, -4)\) (Figure 1.4).

blocks.alt: Grid graph on a pale yellow panel showing x from minus 3 to 0 and y from 0 down to minus 5; the label X is printed at the left end of the x-axis and Y at the top. The downward parabola y = minus 4x squared minus 8x minus 4 touches the x-axis at its vertex, the dot (minus 1, 0), and cuts the y-axis at the dot (0, minus 4).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.4: graph of y = −4x² − 8x − 4 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Factor form \(y = a(x - h)(x - k)\) shows the x-intercepts \(x = h\), \(x = k\) directly.
2. Vertex: \(x = \frac{h+k}{2}\) (halfway between the roots); put this \(x\) into the function for the y-value.
3. \(a > 0\): opens upward, \(y \to +\infty\) at both ends. \(a < 0\): opens downward, \(y \to -\infty\) at both ends.
4. y-intercept: \((0, ahk)\).
5. Repeated factor \(a(x - h)^{2}\): the graph only touches the x-axis at \((h, 0)\), which is the vertex.
6. Plot the intercepts and vertex, use symmetry for an extra point, then join with a smooth curve.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading the root from \((x + 1)\) as \(x = 1\). The root is \(x = -1\) (the sign changes).
2. Forgetting the leading constant: \((2x - 1)(2x + 1) = 4(x - \frac{1}{2})(x + \frac{1}{2})\), so \(a = 4\), and the roots are \(\pm\frac{1}{2}\), not \(\pm 1\).
3. Taking the vertex at one of the intercepts in Case-I. It lies between them, at their average.
4. Drawing a repeated-factor graph crossing the x-axis. It only touches.
5. Drawing a V-shape with a sharp corner. A parabola is a smooth, rounded curve.
